## Estimation

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
- Suppose you want to apply a RV model, there are usually **parameters** you need to estimate to **fit** the model to the data

  - E.g. estimating $p$ for a binomial, or $\mu$ for a normal, etc.

- Estimates are produced using **estimator** functions, i.e. **statistics** of your sample that ideally should converge to the target parameter

  - Law of large numbers useful here
  
  - Method of moments can also be used

- Remember **estimators are RVs** themselves, since they're a function of data, thus also random, with a distribution, expectation, variance, etc..  
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:.5em"}
Generally 2 common types of estimates:

- **Point estimates** are single number estimates of the parameter, i.e. a single "best guess" based on available data

- **Interval estimates**, confidence intervals, are ranges that try to "capture" the true value a certain amount of the time
:::


## Previous coin example cont.

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Continuing from coin flip example from testing chapter, suppose we wish to estimate chance of heads $p$ for a given coin. Experiment:

- Flip it $n$ times and let $X$ be total number of heads,

- We know $X\sim\binom{n,p}$ for known $n$ but unknown $p$.
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:.5em"}
- Define the **estimator** $~\hat p=X/n~$ (which is well-defined), note:

$$
\begin{alignat}{4}
\e{\hat p}&=~~\,\E{\frac Xn}&&=~\frac{\e{X}}n&&=~~~\frac{np}n&&=~~p\\[6pt]
\v{\hat p}&=\V{\frac Xn}&&=\frac{\v{X}}{n^2}&&=\frac{np(1\!-\!p)}{n^2}&&=\frac{p(1\!-\!p)}n
\end{alignat}
$$
:::

:::{.fragment}
- Since $\e{\hat p}\!=\!p$, we say the estimator $\hat p$ is **unbiased**

- Also $\v{\hat p}\!=\!\frac{p(1-p)}n\!\to\!0$ as $n\!\to\!\infty$, so larger sample means more precision
:::


## Bias of estimator

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Let $\hat\theta$ be an estimator for the parameter $\theta$, then its **bias** is defined as:
$$
\bias{\hat\theta,\theta}=\e{\hat\theta}-\theta
$$
I.e. it's the systematic difference between what the estimator produces and the true value
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:1em"}
Since $\e{\hat p}\!-\!p=0$, $\hat p$ is unbiased. Let $p=0.5$. We can find the distribution of $\hat p$ for different $n$ values, with either theory or MC:

```{r,echo=T,eval=T,results='hide'}
# theoretical pmf table of p-hat with p=0.5 for some n
p.hat.theory = \(n,p=0.5) data.frame(p.hat=0:n/n,prob=dbinom(0:n,n,p))

# MC-simulated distribution of p-hat with p=0.5 for some n
p.hat.mc = \(n,p=0.5,M=1e5) rbinom(M,n,p)/n
```

Let's plot both of these for several values of $n$, noting the unbiasedness of the estimator for each value of $n$, as well as how the variance scales with $n$
:::


## $\hat p$ distribution for $n=50$  {transition="slide-in fade-out"}

```{r}
N=50 ; ggplot(p.hat.theory(N)) + geom_col(aes(p.hat,prob),color="black",fill="white") + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=p.hat.mc(N)),aes(x=X,y=..density../N),adjust=2.5,color="red",size=1)    + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(.25,.75),breaks=seq(.25,.75,.05))
```


## $\hat p$ distribution for $n=200$ {transition="fade-in fade-out"}

```{r}
N=200 ; ggplot(p.hat.theory(N)) + geom_col(aes(p.hat,prob),color="black",fill="white") + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=p.hat.mc(N)),aes(x=X,y=..density../N),adjust=2,color="red",size=1)      + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(.25,.75),breaks=seq(.25,.75,.05))
```


## $\hat p$ distribution for $n=800$ {transition="fade-in fade-out"}

```{r}
N=800 ; ggplot(p.hat.theory(N)) + geom_linerange(aes(p.hat,ymin=0,ymax=prob),color="grey50") + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=p.hat.mc(N)),aes(x=X,y=..density../N),adjust=1.5,color="red",size=1)    + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(.25,.75),breaks=seq(.25,.75,.05))
```


## $\hat p$ distribution for $n=3200$ {transition="fade-in slide-out"}

```{r}
N=3200 ; ggplot(p.hat.theory(N)) + geom_linerange(aes(p.hat,ymin=0,ymax=prob),color="grey50") + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=p.hat.mc(N)),aes(x=X,y=..density../N),adjust=1.5,color="red",size=1)    + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(.25,.75),breaks=seq(.25,.75,.05)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(0,.005,.01),labels=c(".000",".005",".010"))
```


## Exercise

Suppose you conducted a simple random sample of 150 people to survey if they prefer candidate A or candidate B for an upcoming local election where voting is mandatory and there's no 3rd option. Out of the 150 people surveyed, 90 preferred A, 60 preferred B.

Estimate the proportion of all residents that would support candidate A over B. Do you expect this estimate to be biased? Estimate the SD of this estimate.

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:1.5em"}
$\hat p=90/150=0.6$. This estimate should be unbiased.

Estimate variance by substituting $\hat p$ for $p$, i.e:
$$
\v{\hat p}=\frac{p(1-p)}n=\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{150}=0.0016
$$
So SD $=0.04$
:::


## Method of moments

<style>#method-of-moments mjx-container[display]{margin:0!important}</style>

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Extending this further, the **method of moments** (MOM) uses the moments of a RV, i.e. $\e{X}$, $\e{X^2}$, $\e{X^3}$, ... to estimate parameters.

Recall $\v{X}=\e{X^2}-(\e{X})^2$, so variance also called the **second central moment**.
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:1.5em"}
Example: suppose we have $X_i$ iid from an exponential distribution with some unknown $\lambda$. We know from theory that:
$$
\bar X\nto\e{X}=\frac1\lambda
$$
Therefore it stands to reason that $\hat\lambda=1/\bar X$ should be a good estimator for $\lambda$
:::

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:1.5em"}
Example: suppose we sample from $X\sim\exp{\lambda=5}$ (ofc normally we don't know $\lambda$). Imagine we repeat the following experiment a large number of times: draw $n=200$ observations, then apply $\hat\lambda=1/\bar X$. What is the sampling distribution of $\hat\lambda$?

```{r}
# estimate lambda across many samples using 1/mean
lambda.hats = replicate(1e4,1/mean(rexp(200,5)))
```
:::


## Exponential example (cont.)

```{r,fig.height=5.5}
hist(lambda.hats) ; abline(v=mean(lambda.hats),col="red",lwd=4)
```


## Exponential example, using SD

Note: since $\sigma^2=1/\lambda^2$, also possible to use (sample SD)^-1^ to estimate $\lambda$, though generally higher moments have more variance, so may be worse, but let's test it!

```{r,fig.height=4.5}
# estimate lambda across many samples using 1/sd
lambda.hats2 = replicate(1e4,1/sd(rexp(200,5)))
hist(lambda.hats2) ; abline(v=mean(lambda.hats2),col="red",lwd=4)
```


## Exponential example, replotting both statistics

```{r}
enframe(c("1/mean"=lambda.hats,"1/sd"=lambda.hats2)) %>% mutate(Estimator=gsub("\\d+$","",name)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value,color=Estimator)) + geom_density(adjust=2,linewidth=1) + xlab("lambda hat") +
  ggtitle("Comparison of 1/mean, 1/sd estimators for exponential lambda parameter")
```


## MOM exercise (gamma dist)

Can also combine moments in expression for more complex problems. Ex:

A Gamma RV takes two parameters, $\alpha,\theta>0$ (shape & scale parameters).  
If $X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\theta)$ we have $\e{X}=\alpha\theta$ and $\v{X}=\alpha\theta^2$.  
Use MOM to define usable $\hat{\theta}$, $\hat{\alpha}$ for the two parameters.

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:1.5em"}
Ans:

1. Since $\v{X}/\e{X}=\theta$, we can use $\hat\theta=S^2/\bar{X}$
2. Since $(\e{X})^2/\v{X}=\alpha$, we can use $\hat\alpha=(\bar{X})^2/S^2$

Other estimators are possible using higher moments or other methods, but these are the simplest using the information available. Demo on next slide.
:::


## MOM exercise (gamma dist) cont.

```{r,fig.height=5}
# pick some arbitrary shape/scale parameters and plot gamma (alpha=3,theta=2)
plot(\(x)dgamma(x,shape=3,scale=2),from=0,to=20,main="PDF of Gamma(shape=3,scale=2)")
```


## MOM exercise (gamma dist) cont.

```{r,include=F}
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(3,3,3,0),mgp=c(2,.6,0))
```
```{r,fig.height=4.5}
# draw many samples of n=100 and check results of estimators are good (alpha=3,theta=2)
estimates = replicate(1e4, { x=rgamma(100,shape=3,scale=2); c(var(x)/mean(x),mean(x)^2/var(x)) })
alpha.hats = estimates[2,] ; theta.hats = estimates[1,]
hist(alpha.hats) ; abline(v=mean(alpha.hats),col="red",lwd=4)
hist(theta.hats) ; abline(v=mean(theta.hats),col="red",lwd=4)
```
```{r,include=F}
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```


## Interval estimates

Often, want to know how good a point estimate is, can use **confidence interval** instead

Review exercise: continuing from previous exercise where 90/150 people surveyed preferred candidate A to B. Give a 95% confidence interval for this result.

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:1em"}
Ans: $\hat p=0.6$ with estimated SD, or **standard error** (SE) of $0.04$. To get 95% confidence interval, need about $2\times$ SE on either side of estimate, so about $(0.52,0.68)$
:::

:::: {.columns .fragment}

::: {.column width="40%"}

MC version: resimulate with $p\!=\!\hat p$, then find 95% central band of new resimulated point estimates

```{r}
new.X = rbinom(1e5,150,90/150)
new.phats = new.X/150
(ci = quantile(new.phats,c(.025,.975)))
```
```{r,eval=F}
hist(new.phats)
abline(v=ci, col="red", lwd=3)
```

:::

:::{.column width="60%"}

```{r,echo=F,fig.width=6,fig.height=4}
hist(new.phats)
abline(v=ci, col="red", lwd=3)
```

:::

::::


## Wait what? MC interval explained

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Why does this work? Suppose we are trying to estimate a parameter $\theta$ with our observed sample statistic $S$. After fitting with $S$, we resimulate to get a new set of statistics $S^*$. One can check these are generally approximately true with typical sample sizes:

1. $\e{S^*}=S$
2. $\v{S^*}\approx\v{S}$
3. $S^*$ symmetric about $\e{S^*}$
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1}
Together, these properties imply that the **distribution of $S^*$ around $S$ is _similar_ to the distribution of $S$ around $\theta$**. Thus, resimulating $S^*$ around $S$ estimates the variability of $S$, which is used to compute the CI.

This is a highly simplified argument. For more mathematical details, see Karl Rohe's writeup [here](https://karlrohe.github.io/340-Spring21/text/chapter_04_estimation/LogicOfStatisticalEstimation.html#what-makes-this-logic-logical). Visual demo on next page...
:::


## Demo of MC interval

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Suppose we sample $n=100$ from a known normal RV with unknown $\mu=10$, $\sigma^2=2^2$. We observe the following sample statistics:

```{r,include=F}
set.seed(1)
```
```{r}
x = rnorm(100, 10, 2) ; c(mean(x), sd(x))
```
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1}
Thus, $S=\bar X\approx`r round(mean(x),2)`$. Then, we resimulate many times using $S$ to get distribution of $S^*$:

```{r}
new.means = replicate(1e4,mean(rnorm(100,mean(x),sd(x)))) ; c(ms<-mean(new.means),ss<-sd(new.means))
```
:::

:::{.fragment}
Compare distribution of $S=\bar X$ around $\mu=10$ with distribution of $S^*$ around $S\approx`r round(mean(x),2)`$

```{r ci.plot,eval=F}
# adjust=3.5 smoothes out S* a bit more, but distorts the density curve,
# hence quantiles of S* later plotted with ±z=2.2 to match distorted density
ggplot() + geom_function(aes(color="S"),fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),xlim=c(9.2,10.8),linewidth=1.5) + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=new.means),aes(X,color="S*"),adjust=3.5,linewidth=1.5,key_glyph="path") +
  geom_linerange(aes(x=c(10,mean(x))),ymin=0,ymax=1.99) + labs(color="Statistic",x=NULL,y=NULL) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),geom="area",xlim=c(9.2,9.6),fill="#1d9d79",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),geom="area",xlim=c(10.4,10.8),fill="#1d9d79",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,ms,ss*1.12),geom="area",xlim=ms+ss*c(-4,-2.2),fill="#d76420",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,ms,ss*1.12),geom="area",xlim=ms+ss*c(2.2,4),fill="#d76420",alpha=.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(9.2,10.8,.2),minor_breaks=NULL,expand=0) + 
  scale_y_continuous(expand=0,limits=c(0,2.1))
```
:::


## Demo of MC interval (cont.)  {transition="slide-in fade-out"}

```{r,ref.label='ci.plot',eval=T,echo=F,fig.height=4}
```

- Green curve is theoretical distribution of $S\!=\!\bar X\!\sim\!\norm{10,2^2/100}$ about $\mu\!=\!10$
- Orange curve is simulated distribution of $S^*$ about observed sample mean $\bar X\!\approx\!`r round(mean(x),2)`$
- Note two curves have similar shape/width, just shifted
- 95% of time, $\bar X\!\in\!(9.6,10.4)$, so that quantiles of $S^*$, taken as CI, contains $\mu\!=\!10$


## Demo of MC interval (cont.)  {transition="fade-in slide-out"}

```{r,echo=F,fig.height=4}
set.seed(286) ; x = rnorm(100, 10, 2)
new.means = replicate(1e4,mean(rnorm(100,mean(x),sd(x)))) ; ms=mean(new.means) ; ss=sd(new.means)
ggplot() + geom_function(aes(color="S"),fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),xlim=c(9.2,10.8),linewidth=1.5) + 
  geom_density(data=tibble(X=new.means),aes(X,color="S*"),adjust=2,linewidth=1.5,key_glyph="path") +
  geom_linerange(aes(x=c(10,mean(x))),ymin=0,ymax=1.99) + labs(color="Statistic",x=NULL,y=NULL) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),geom="area",xlim=c(9.2,9.6),fill="#1d9d79",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,10,2/10),geom="area",xlim=c(10.4,10.8),fill="#1d9d79",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,ms,ss*1.04),geom="area",xlim=ms+ss*c(-4,-2.1),fill="#d76420",alpha=.5) +
  stat_function(fun=\(x)dnorm(x,ms,ss*1.04),geom="area",xlim=ms+ss*c(2.1,4),fill="#d76420",alpha=.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(9.2,10.8,.2),minor_breaks=NULL,expand=0) + 
  scale_y_continuous(expand=0,limits=c(0,2.1))
```

- 5% of the time, $\bar X\notin(9.6,10.4)$, and quantiles of $S^*$ taken as CI won't contain $\mu=10$
- Here, in this "unlucky" rerun, observed sample mean $\bar X\!\approx\!`r round(mean(x),2)`$
- This is outside the central 95% range of $S$, so the quantiles of $S^*$ don't contain $\mu$

Similar argument/demo approximately applies to other RVs too, not just normal


## Generalized MC confidence interval steps:

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
1. Identify RV **model** & **parameter(s)** for data
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1}
2. Pick point **estimator** function (e.g. using LLN, MOM, or other method)
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
3. Apply estimator to get initial **point estimate** (S)
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
4. Assume true parameter equals point estimate, then **resimulate** many times, each time:
   - Generate **new dataset of same size as original**,
   - Compute new point estimate ($S^*$) of newly generated data.
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
5. Take appropriate quantiles of $S^*$ distribution as **confidence interval**.
:::

:::{.fragment}
6. Interpret results in context of original question!
   - E.g. "We are 95% confident that true [parameter] is in [interval]."
:::


## Exercise:

Suppose we have the following $n=30$ observations from a Poisson distribution:

```{r,echo=F}
set.seed(1)
x = rpois(30,8)
```

> `r toString(x)`

1. What's a good point estimator function?

2. Give a point estimate of the rate parameter $\lambda$.

3. Find a 95% confidence interval for $\lambda$.

Answer in steps:

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:-.5em"}
1. Sample mean works great here. Variance also works, but will have higher SE.
:::

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:-.7em"}
2. Find sample mean $\bar X\approx`r round(mean(x),2)`$.
:::

:::{.fragment}
```{r}
# 3. repeatedly generate n=30 new poisson points and find new lambda hats, then take quantiles
new.lambda.hats = replicate(1e4,mean(rpois(30,mean(x))))
quantile(new.lambda.hats,c(.025,.975))
```
:::

## Applied example: mark & recapture

More interesting example. In ecology, [mark & recapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_and_recapture) is a common technique to estimate the population of a species of animals where a 1^st^ sample is marked and released, then later a 2^nd^ sample is taken and the number already marked is counted. Assume in both samples, any animal in population is **equally likely** to be captured. &nbsp; [Let:]{.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

:::{.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
- $N$ be total number of animals in population
- $n$ be number of animals marked in 1^st^ sample
- $K$ be number of animals captured in 2^nd^ sample
- $k$ be number of animals in 2^nd^ sample that are marked
:::

:::{.fragment}
Under assumption, $k/K=n/N$, so an estimator could be $\hat{N}=nK/k$. This is called the Lincoln–Petersen estimator.

Ex: You're studying walleyes in Lake Mendota. You catch & mark 500 fish. A few weeks later, you catch another 500, 12 of which were already marked. Give a point estimate for the total walleye population $N$ in the lake. &nbsp; [**Ans:** using estimator, $\hat N=500^2/12\approx20833$.]{.fragment}
:::

## Applied example: mark & recapture (cont.)

Next, use MC to find a 95% confidence interval for your estimate (follow the checklist!)

(*answer in steps*) First, simulate one new "observed" $k$ for $N=\hat N$:

:::{.fragment style="margin-top:1em"}
Different ways to simulate:

```{r}
# suppose first 1-500 of fish are marked, then can simulate n using sample()
sim = \(N,n=500,K=500) sum(sample(N,K)<=n)
sim(20833)
# can also approximate with rbinom(), i.e. each fish modeled as n/N chance of being marked
sim2 = \(N,n=500,K=500,M=1) rbinom(M,K,n/N)
sim2(20833)
# can even approximate with rpois(), i.e. draw fish with averate rate of n*K/N
sim3 = \(N,n=500,K=500,M=1) rpois(M,n*K/N)
sim3(20833)
```

Can we check if all three of these give similar results?
:::


## Applied example: mark & recapture (cont.)

```{r}
# can check all three are comparable
tibble(x=c(replicate(1e4,sim(20833)),sim2(20833,M=1e4),sim3(20833,M=1e4)),
       type=rep(c("sample","binom","pois"),each=1e4)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x)) + facet_grid(type~.) + geom_bar()
```


## Applied example: mark & recapture (cont.)

Next, repeat this many times, each time computing $\hat N$, then take quantiles as CI

:::{.fragment}
```{r,fig.height=4}
# using sample()
N.hats = 500^2/replicate(1e4,sim(20833))
quantile(N.hats,c(.025,.975))
# using rbinom()
N.hats = 500^2/sim2(20833,M=1e4)
quantile(N.hats,c(.025,.975))
# using rpois()
N.hats = 500^2/sim3(20833,M=1e4)
quantile(N.hats,c(.025,.975))
```
All methods give same 95% CI for $N$ of $(13158,41667)$.
:::


## Another applied example: German Tank problem

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
During WWII, some parts of captured German tanks were found to likely have sequential serial numbers. This gave rise to an [interesting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_tank_problem): given a sample of sequential serial numbers, can we statistically estimate the total number of tanks?

```{r echo=F,eval=T}
set.seed(15)
true.num = 425 ; n = 10
serials = sample(true.num,n)
```

:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:1em"}

Suppose we have the following set of `r n` serial numbers from captured tanks below. Model the true population of serial numbers as Discrete Uniform$(1,N)$ where $N$ is the true total number of tanks. Come up with at least 2 different sensible estimators for $N$.

> `r toString(serials)`

:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}

Ans: the natural thing to try is the sample max, for a second option can use MOM since we know expectation $\mu=(N+1)/2$ we can use $\hat N=2\cdot\bar X-1$

```{r}
# data is in vector serials, sample size set to n, compute point estimates
( N.max = max(serials) )
( N.mom = 2*mean(serials)-1 )
```

Can you now find a 95% confidence interval?
:::


## German Tank problem Confidence interval

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Sample max works poorly for CI, since using point estimate as true $N$ then resampling generally gives lower MC resimulated sample max, due to its inherent biasedness

```{r}
N.max.resim = replicate(1e5, max(sample(N.max,n)))  # try max for CI, but result doesn't
quantile(N.max.resim, c(.025, .975))                # even contain original point estimate!
N.mom.resim = replicate(1e5, 2*mean(sample(N.mom,n))-1)  # MOM estimator is ok though,
quantile(N.mom.resim, c(.025,.975))                      # doesn't run into same issue
```

Follow up: can be shown minimum-variance unbiased estimator (MVUE) is $M(1\!+\frac1n)\!-\!1$ where $M$, $n$ are sample maximum and size. Find the MVUE point & interval estimates
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1}
```{r}
mvue = \(x) max(x)*(1+1/length(x))-1  # define estimator function for ease
( N.mvue = mvue(serials) )
N.mvue.resim = replicate(1e5, mvue(sample(N.mvue,n)))
quantile(N.mvue.resim, c(.025,.975))
```
:::


## CLT-based confidence intervals

:::{.fragment .no-fade-in .semi-fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
Can also use CLT for CI for the true mean. Suppose $X$ is some RV (not necessarily normal) with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Generally, if you have $\approx30$ observations or more, sample mean $\bar X$ can be treated as approx. normal with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$ even if $X$ isn't normal. Then, an approx. 95% CI for $\mu$ is $\bar X\pm 1.96 \cdot S/\sqrt n$ where $S$ is sample SD

```{r eval=T,echo=F}
set.seed(1) ; n=30 ; true.lambda = 10/60
x = round(rexp(n,true.lambda),1)
```
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out data-fragment-index=1}
Example: we have a sample of `r n` wait times in minutes between customers walking into a coffee shop one morning. Find 95% CI for $\mu$ then use this to find CI for $\lambda$

> `r toString(x)` ($\bar X=`r round(mean(x),2)`$, $S=`r round(sd(x),2)`$)

:::

:::{.fragment}
```{r}
# 95% CI for true mean mu
( ci = mean(x) + c(-1,1) * 1.96 * sd(x)/sqrt(length(x)) )
```

Note since $\mu=1/\lambda$, we can take the reciprocal of the bounds to get CI for $\lambda$

```{r}
( 1 / ci ) * 60  # convert to more natural rate of customers per hour
```
:::


## Testing/confidence equivalence

Finally as a topic, you can use a confidence interval to conduct an equivalent level test. E.g. suppose you want to test if some parameter $\theta=0$ vs $\ne0$ at $\alpha=0.05$.

This is equivalent checking if a 95% confidence interval for $\theta$ includes 0 or not.

If one-sided alternative used instead with same $\alpha$, equivalent to checking if 90% confidence interval includes 0.

 - Short page on [MSE of estimators & bias-variance decomposition](https://pages.stat.wisc.edu/~bwu62/MSE_estimators.html)
